chapters.title: Chapter 7: Capstone: Building and Defending a Capacity-Aware Scaling Plan

lessons.title: How Capacity Questions Show Up in Quant and Prop Trading Interviews

children.text: Chapter 1 mentioned that capacity questions come up often in quant and prop trading interviews. This lesson goes deep on exactly what those questions tend to look like, and how to structure an answer that shows real understanding rather than memorized vocabulary.
Why Interviewers Ask About Capacity At All

A capacity question is rarely really about capacity. It is a quick way to check whether a candidate treats a strategy as a business decision, one with real size, real execution, and real limits, or purely as a research result to be reported and defended. Candidates who have only ever backtested strategies at whatever size their laptop could handle often have never been forced to think about this at all, which makes it an efficient question for an interviewer to ask.

cells: How would you estimate this strategy's capacity?
ADV, a participation cap, the square-root law, and how turnover adjusts the result
This backtest looks amazing at small size, what happens at Rs X crore?
Impact cost scaling with size, the turnover penalty, and possible universe or style drift as size grows
How do you know if a strategy has stopped working versus just had a bad month?
Rolling IC or a similar decay signal, sample size, and distinguishing genuine decay from ordinary noise
What would worry you about two "different" strategies that look uncorrelated?
Position overlap, not just return correlation, and whether both could get hit by the same forced-selling event
Walk me through executing a large order in an illiquid stock
Participation caps, TWAP, VWAP, or POV, and benchmarking against implementation shortfall
When would you tell a PM to stop raising capital for a strategy?
A concrete capacity ceiling, diminishing marginal benefit, and the fee-driven incentive to keep raising anyway

children.text: A Framework for Answering Any Capacity Question On the Spot

cells: 1. Define capacity for this strategy
State in one sentence what capacity means here, such as the AUM at which risk-adjusted returns fall below an acceptable threshold
2. Name the key inputs
ADV, turnover, volatility, and any known crowding or replicability concern
3. Sketch the relationship
Even a rough version of the square-root law and the turnover-squared effect shows you can actually compute something, not just describe it
4. Name a caveat
Point to at least one real limitation, such as model uncertainty, crowding, or a stress scenario, to show you are not overconfident in a single number

body.title: Structuring a Real Interview Answer
body.scenario: In a quant interview, you are shown a backtest of a small-cap strategy that achieved 40% CAGR on Rs 5 lakh of simulated capital over three years. The interviewer asks: if we ran this strategy with Rs 20 crore instead, what would you expect to happen, and why?
body.prompt: How would you structure your answer?
body.modelAnswer: Start by naming the concept directly: at Rs 5 lakh, the strategy's own trading is too small to move any stock's price, so the backtest is really measuring a frictionless version of the strategy. At Rs 20 crore, position sizes would likely represent a meaningful share of average daily volume in many of the underlying small-cap names, so real impact cost, using something like the square-root law, would start eating into returns. If the strategy also trades frequently, that effect gets much worse, since capacity falls with the square of turnover, not in proportion to it. I would want to know the strategy's typical position size relative to ADV, its turnover, and whether its signal is public or easily replicated, since crowding could compress returns further even before considering the trader's own impact. My expectation is that realized CAGR at Rs 20 crore would likely be well below 40%, possibly in the single digits to low teens depending on those inputs, and I would want to actually estimate a capacity ceiling rather than guess.

body.text: Four answers reliably signal inexperience in a capacity conversation: treating whether a strategy works and whether it scales as the same claim, assuming a liquid universe like the Nifty 50 automatically means unlimited capacity without asking about turnover, describing capacity only in vague terms without naming a single input or formula, and discussing scaling without mentioning execution at all. Naming at least ADV, turnover, and one honest caveat is usually enough to separate a considered answer from a guess.

A capacity question is an invitation to show you think about strategies the way a real desk has to, not the way a backtest report does. Naming the right inputs, sketching the right relationship, and admitting a real caveat will get you further than any amount of confident hand-waving.

points: Capacity questions test whether a candidate treats a strategy as something that has to hold real capital and execute in real markets, not just as a research result.

Common question patterns cover estimating capacity, extrapolating a small backtest to scale, distinguishing decay from noise, spotting hidden overlap between strategies, executing at size, and knowing when to stop raising capital.

A simple four-step template, define capacity for this strategy, name the key inputs, sketch the relationship, name a caveat, works as a reliable structure for almost any capacity question asked on the spot.

The clearest signals of inexperience are conflating working with scaling, assuming liquidity alone guarantees capacity, staying vague instead of naming a concrete input or formula, and leaving execution out of a scaling discussion entirely.
